planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in early spring before bud break, in partial shade while young; in zone 9 plant February–March. Pawpaws resent root disturbance, so handle the fleshy taproot carefully and avoid moving established trees.

directions: Plant in partial shade while young, transitioning the tree into full sun as it matures, and site alongside a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar since Tallahatchie will not set fruit on its own. Selected by pawpaw breeder Neal Peterson from a seedling growing in his Maryland research orchard, Tallahatchie produces medium-large fruit averaging around 9 ounces with an unusually low seed content and a smooth, silky texture that has made it a favorite for pawpaw ice cream and custard. Its floral, mellow flavor ripens mid-to-late season, and the tree tends to set fruit in generous clusters of five or more, so growers in warm zone 7-8 gardens may want to thin heavy clusters for more even ripening. Give it deep, well-drained soil and consistent moisture during establishment, since pawpaw's fleshy taproot resents both drought and transplant disturbance.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Program — Pawpaw Cultivars

common_name: Halvin's Sidewinder Pawpaw (Cold-Hardy Wild-Selected Iowa Pawpaw)

planting.note: Plant a container-grown tree in early spring in rich, well-drained soil, with light shade for the first year or two before transitioning to full sun. A second, unrelated pawpaw cultivar is required nearby for pollination.

directions: Plant a container-grown tree in early spring in rich, well-drained soil with some shade for the first year or two, then let full sun take over as the canopy fills in; a second, unrelated pawpaw cultivar is required nearby for pollination, since Halvin's Sidewinder cannot set fruit with its own pollen. Found growing wild in southwestern Iowa by Tyler and Danae Halvin, this selection stood out for exceptional cold hardiness and reliably early ripening, qualities that also translate into vigorous, trouble-free growth through the long hot summers of zone 7-9 gardens. Fruits run 8 to 14 ounces with smooth, sweet flesh carrying a distinct hint of pineapple and none of the bitter aftertaste some wild pawpaws show. The tree stays a manageable 15 to 20 feet tall and wide, making it easier to net or hand-thin than some larger-growing named cultivars.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Program — Pawpaw Cultivars
Iowa State University Extension and Outreach — Pawpaw Production
North Carolina State University Extension — Pawpaw Production Guide

common_name: Summer Delight Pawpaw (Very Early-Ripening Low-Seed Pawpaw)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in early spring before bud break, in partial shade while young; in zone 9 plant February–March. Plant a second, genetically different pawpaw cultivar nearby for pollination.

directions: Site in partial shade for the first season or two, moving to full sun as the tree matures, and plant a second, genetically different pawpaw cultivar nearby, since Summer Delight needs cross-pollination to bear a full crop. Bred by Kentucky nurseryman Cliff England as a cross of two respected parents, Sunflower and Overleese, this selection was developed specifically to ripen weeks ahead of most pawpaw cultivars, often coloring up in late July in warm climates and giving Southern growers the earliest homegrown pawpaws of the season. The 7 to 12 ounce fruits have notably thick, durable skin, a very low seed count, and rich golden flesh with a balanced mango-pineapple flavor rather than the heavier sweetness of some late-season types. Because it ripens so early, Summer Delight is a useful complement to mid- and late-season cultivars for extending the pawpaw harvest window in zone 7-9 orchards.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Program — Pawpaw Cultivars

common_name: Elmo American Persimmon (Large Spot-Free Claypool Selection)

planting.note: Plant a grafted bare-root or container tree in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil; Elmo is not self-fertile and needs a second American persimmon nearby for reliable fruit set.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, and site a second American persimmon nearby, since Elmo is not self-fertile and needs cross-pollination to bear a reliable crop — only self-fertile selections such as Meader or Yates can be grown alone. Developed as a hand-pollinated cross of Golden Supreme and Garretson and originally released under the breeding designation Claypool A-118, Elmo was chosen for its large, richly flavored orange fruit that stays notably free of the black surface spotting that can mar other American persimmon selections. Fruit ripens October into November and, like all American persimmons, must fully soften after a hard frost before the astringency disappears and the deep, honeyed sweetness comes through. Elmo is a consistently heavy bearer once established and tolerates the heat, humidity, and clay soils typical of zone 7-9 Southern gardens with little more than watering during its first two seasons.
sources: Purdue University Extension — Persimmon Cultivars

common_name: Prairie Dawn American Persimmon (Early-Ripening Seedless Claypool Selection)

planting.note: Plant a grafted bare-root or container tree in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil; Prairie Dawn sets fruit on its own but crops more heavily with a second American persimmon nearby.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in full sun on deep, well-drained soil; Prairie Dawn sets a crop on its own but bears more heavily with a second American persimmon or a known male tree planted nearby for cross-pollination. Bred by Illinois hobbyist Jim Claypool under the designation H55A, Prairie Dawn was selected for cold hardiness well beyond what most Southern growers need, but that same toughness translates into vigorous, dependable growth and disease resistance through the long, humid summers of zone 7-9. It is one of the earliest-ripening American persimmon cultivars, coloring up by late September with large, seedless, orange-yellow fruit that is sweet and firm rather than watery. Prune annually to hold the naturally tall tree to a manageable 12 feet or so, since it can reach 20 feet or more if left alone, and expect the first meaningful crops within two to three years of planting a grafted tree.
sources: Purdue University Extension — Persimmon Cultivars
University of Illinois Extension — Fruit Production
Northern Nut Growers Association

common_name: Prairie Gem American Persimmon (Tender-Fleshed Seedless Claypool Selection)

planting.note: Plant a grafted bare-root or container tree in late winter to early spring in average to well-drained soil; Prairie Gem sets fruit on its own but crops more heavily with a second American persimmon nearby.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in average to well-drained soil; Prairie Gem produces fruit on a single tree but crops more heavily with a second American persimmon or a male seedling nearby to complete pollination. A sibling selection to Prairie Dawn from Jim Claypool's Illinois breeding work, Prairie Gem carries the same exceptional cold hardiness but ripens its light orange, seedless fruit slightly later, typically in the early-to-mid fall window. The tender, sweet flesh softens to a texture much like a ripe tomato when ready to eat, and trees are notably free of the pests and diseases that trouble many other fruit species in humid Southern gardens. Keep it pruned to about 12 feet for easy harvest, since Prairie Gem will otherwise grow taller, and expect bearing to begin within two to three years of setting out a grafted tree.
sources: Purdue University Extension — Persimmon Cultivars

common_name: Lehman's Delight American Persimmon (Large Self-Fertile Indiana Selection)

planting.note: Plant a grafted bare-root or container tree in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained to average soil; Lehman's Delight is self-fertile and sets a full crop on a single tree.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in deep, well-drained to average soil; Lehman's Delight is self-fertile and will set a full crop on a single tree, though a second American persimmon nearby can further boost yields. Bred by Indiana persimmon breeder Jerry Lehman and also sold under its original breeding number, 100-46, it was one of Lehman's own favorite selections from thousands of controlled crosses for combining outstanding size, flavor, and productivity. The large, reddish-orange fruit — often exceeding two inches across — has smooth, clear pulp and an intensely sweet flavor once fully soft-ripe after frost, and mature trees are known as some of the heaviest-bearing American persimmon selections available. It stays comparatively compact for the species, tolerates the heat and clay soils common across zone 7-9 gardens, and needs little upkeep beyond removing root suckers once established.
sources: Purdue University Extension — Persimmon Cultivars
